{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
[[Image:Rgamma plot real.svg|thumb|250px|Plot of {{sfrac|1|Γ(''x'')}} along the real axis]]

[[File:Reciprocal-gamma-domain-coloring.png|right|thumb|250px|Reciprocal gamma function {{math|{{sfrac|1|Γ(''z'')}}}} in the [[complex plane]], plotted using [[domain coloring]].]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''reciprocal gamma function''' is the [[special function|function]]
<math display=block>f(z) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(z)},</math>
where {{math|Γ(''z'')}} denotes the [[gamma function]]. Since the gamma function is [[meromorphic function|meromorphic]] and nonzero everywhere in the [[complex plane]], its reciprocal is an [[entire function]]. As an entire function, it is of order 1 (meaning that {{math|log log {{abs|{{sfrac|1|Γ(''z'')}}}}}} grows no faster than {{math|log {{abs|''z''}}}}), but of infinite type (meaning that {{math|log {{abs|{{sfrac|1|Γ(''z'')}}}}}} grows faster than any multiple of {{math|{{abs|''z''}}}}, since its growth is approximately proportional to {{math|{{abs|''z''}} log {{abs|''z''}}}} in the left-half plane).

The reciprocal is sometimes used as a starting point for [[numerical analysis|numerical computation]] of the gamma function, and a few software libraries provide it separately from the regular gamma function.

[[Karl Weierstrass]] called the reciprocal gamma function the "factorielle" and used it in his development of the [[Weierstrass factorization theorem]].

== Infinite product expansion ==
Following from the [[infinite product]] definitions for the [[gamma function]], due to [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] and [[Karl Weierstrass|Weierstrass]] respectively, we get the following infinite product expansion for the reciprocal gamma function:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)} &=  z \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1+\frac{z}{n}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^z} \\
\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)} &= z e^{\gamma z} \prod_{n=1}^\infty \left(1 + \frac{z}{n}\right) e^{-\frac{z}{n}}
\end{align}</math>

where {{math|''γ'' {{=}} 0.577216...}} is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].  These expansions are valid for all complex numbers&nbsp;{{math|''z''}}.

== Taylor series ==
[[Taylor series]] expansion around {{math|0}} gives:<ref>{{cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Gamma function |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |lang=en |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GammaFunction.html |access-date=2021-06-15}}</ref>
<math display=block>\frac{1}{\ \Gamma(z)\ } = z + \gamma\ z^2 + \left(\frac{\gamma^2}{2} - \frac{\pi^2}{12}\right)\ z^3 + \left(\frac{\gamma^3}{6} - \frac{\gamma\pi^2}{12} + \frac{\zeta(3)}{3}\ \right)z^4 + \cdots\ </math>
where {{math|''γ''}} is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]]. For {{math|''n'' > 2}}, the coefficient {{math|''a''<sub>''n''</sub>}} for the {{math|''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}} term can be computed recursively as<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wrench |first=J.W. |year=1968 |title=Concerning two series for the gamma function |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=22 |issue=103 |pages=617–626 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1968-0237078-4 |s2cid=121472614 |doi-access=free }} and {{br}}{{cite journal |last=Wrench |first=J.W. |year=1973 |title=Erratum: Concerning two series for the gamma function |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=27 |issue=123 |pages=681–682 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1973-0319344-9 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Fekih-Ahmed2014/>
<math display=block>a_n = \frac{\ {a_2\ a_{n-1} + \sum_{j=2}^{n-1} (-1)^{j+1}\ \zeta(j)\ a_{n-j}}\ }{n-1} = \frac{\ \gamma\ a_{n-1} - \zeta(2)\ a_{n-2} + \zeta(3)\ a_{n-3}-\cdots\ }{n-1}</math>
where {{math|''ζ''}} is the [[Riemann zeta function]]. An integral representation for these coefficients was recently found by Fekih-Ahmed (2014):<ref name=Fekih-Ahmed2014>{{cite web |last=Fekih-Ahmed |first=L. |year=2014 |title=On the power series expansion of the reciprocal gamma function |website=HAL archives |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01029331v1}}</ref>
<math display=block>a_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{\pi n!}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\ \operatorname{Im}\Bigl[\ \bigl( \log(t)-i\pi \bigr)^n\ \Bigr]\ \mathrm{d} t ~.</math>

Fekih-Ahmed (2014)<ref name=Fekih-Ahmed2014/> also gives an approximation for {{math|''a''<sub>''n''</sub>}}:

<!-- Original form --
<math display=block>a_n \approx (-1)^n \sqrt{\frac{ 2 }{ \pi }\ } \frac{\sqrt{n\ }}{n!} 
\ \operatorname\mathcal{I_m} \left( \frac{\ z_0^{(1/2-n)}\ e^{-n z_0}\ }{\sqrt{ 1 + z_0\ }} \right)\ ,</math> --><!-- Equivalent -->
<math display=block>a_n \approx \frac{(-1)^n}{\ (n-1)!\ } \ \sqrt{ \frac{2}{\ \pi n \ }\ }\ 
\operatorname{Im} \left( \frac{\ z_0^{\left( 1/2 - n \right)}\ e^{-n z_0}\ }{\sqrt{ 1 + z_0\ }} \right)\ ,</math> 
where {{math|1=''z''<sub>0</sub> = −1/''n'' exp(''W''<sub>−1</sub>(−''n''))}}, and {{math|''W''<sub>−1</sub>}} is the negative-first branch of the [[Lambert W function|Lambert {{math|''W''}} function]].

The Taylor expansion around {{math|1}} has the same (but shifted) coefficients, i.e.:
<math display=block>\frac{1}{\Gamma(1+z)} = \frac{1}{z\Gamma(z)} = 1 + \gamma\ z + \left(\frac{\gamma^2}{2} - \frac{\pi^2}{12}\right)\ z^2 + \left(\frac{\gamma^3}{6} - \frac{\gamma\pi^2}{12} + \frac{\zeta(3)}{3}\ \right)z^3 + \cdots\ </math>
(the reciprocal of [[Gamma function#Pi function|Gauss's pi function]]).

== Asymptotic expansion ==
As {{math|{{abs|''z''}}}} goes to infinity at a constant {{math|arg(''z'')}} we have:
<math display=block>\ln (1/\Gamma(z)) \sim -z \ln (z) + z + \tfrac{1}{2} \ln \left (\frac{z}{2\pi} \right ) - \frac{1}{12z} + \frac{1}{360z^3} -\frac{1}{1260 z^5}\qquad \text{for}~ \left|\arg(z)\right| < \pi</math>

== Contour integral representation ==
An integral representation due to [[Hermann Hankel]] is
<math display=block>\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)} = \frac{i}{2\pi} \oint_H (-t)^{-z} e^{-t} \, dt,</math>
where {{math|''H''}} is the [[Hankel contour]], that is, the path encircling 0 in the positive direction, beginning at and returning to positive infinity with respect for the [[branch cut]] along the positive real axis. According to Schmelzer & Trefethen,<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Thomas |last1=Schmelzer |author2-link=Lloyd N. Trefethen |first2=Lloyd N. |last2=Trefethen |year=2007 |title=Computing the Gamma function using contour integrals and rational approximations |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=558–571 |doi=10.1137/050646342 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/050646342|url-access=subscription }};
{{cite web |title=Copy on Trefethen's academic website |website=Mathematics, Oxford, UK |url=https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/publication/PDF/2007_122.pdf |access-date=2020-08-03}};
{{cite CiteSeerX |title=Link to two other copies |citeseerx=10.1.1.210.299 }}</ref> numerical evaluation of Hankel's integral is the basis of some of the best methods for computing the gamma function.

== Integral representations at the positive integers ==

For positive integers {{math|''n'' ≥ 1}}, there is an integral for the reciprocal [[factorial]] function given by<ref>{{cite book|last1=Graham, Knuth, and Patashnik|title=Concrete Mathematics|date=1994|publisher=Addison-Wesley|page=566}}</ref> 
<math display=block>\frac{1}{n!} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{-nit} e^{e^{it}}\ dt.</math>

Similarly, for any real {{math|''c'' > 0}} and {{math|''z'' ∈ '''C'''}} such that {{math|Re(''z'') > 0}} we have the next integral for the reciprocal gamma function along the real axis in the form of:<ref>
{{cite journal |last1= Schmidt|first1= Maxie D.|date= 2019-05-19|title=A Short Note on Integral Transformations and Conversion Formulas for Sequence Generating Functions  |journal=Axioms |volume= 8|issue=2 |pages=62 |doi=10.3390/axioms8020062 |doi-access= free|arxiv=1809.03933}}</ref> 
<math display=block>\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (c+ it)^{-z} e^{c+it} dt, </math> 
where the particular case when {{math|1=''z'' = ''n'' + 1/2}} provides a corresponding relation for the reciprocal [[double factorial]] function,
<math display=block>\frac{1}{(2n-1)!!} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2^n \cdot \Gamma\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)}.</math>

== Integral along the real axis ==

Integration of the reciprocal gamma function along the positive real axis gives the value
<math display=block>\int_{0}^\infty \frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\, dx \approx 2.80777024,</math>
which is known as the [[Fransén&ndash;Robinson constant]].<ref>{{cite OEIS|A058655|Decimal expansion of area under the curve 1/Gamma(x) from zero to infinity}}</ref>

We have the following formula<ref>{{cite book |author= Henri Cohen|date=2007 |title=Number Theory Volume II: Analytic and Modern Tools  |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-49894-2 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=240 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-49894-2 |isbn=978-0-387-49893-5 |issn=0072-5285}}</ref>{{rp|ch 9,exercise 100}}
<math display=block>\int_0^\infty \dfrac{a^x}{\Gamma(x)}\,dx=ae^a+a\int_0^\infty\dfrac{e^{-ax}}{\log^2(x)+\pi^2}\,dx</math>
